title: Scope Functions & Extensions
scopeHtml: Scope: let/run/with/apply/also/takeIf/takeUnless, choosing between them and readability, and extension functions and properties (dispatch, resolution, visibility, companion and member extensions). Inline mechanics, lambdas with receiver as a DSL concept, and smart-cast rules are covered in their own chunks.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through let, run, with, apply and also. How do they differ?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the most common Kotlin screening question. They want to hear the two axes, not a memorized table. Mixing up what each one returns is an instant red flag.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: All five run a block on an object, and they differ on two axes. First, how the block sees the object: as this (run, with, apply) or as it (let, also). Second, what the call returns: the lambda result (let, run, with) or the object itself (apply, also). with is the only one that isn't an extension; you pass the object in as an argument. They're all inline, so they cost nothing at runtime. The choice is about readability and intent.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
These are plain stdlib functions. They're not language keywords. Their signatures (Kotlin stdlib, Standard.kt) explain everything:

inline fun <T, R> T.let(block: (T) -> R): R
inline fun <T, R> T.run(block: T.() -> R): R
inline fun <T, R> with(receiver: T, block: T.() -> R): R
inline fun <T> T.apply(block: T.() -> Unit): T
inline fun <T> T.also(block: (T) -> Unit): T
  • (T) -> R means the object is passed as a parameter, so it's named it by default and you can rename it.
  • T.() -> R is a lambda with receiver, so the object becomes this and its members are reachable without a qualifier.
  • Returning T means the call evaluates to the original object, so it chains like a builder. Returning R means it evaluates to the last expression of the lambda.
                 returns lambda result      returns context object
 object as it    let                        also
 object as this  run, with                  apply

Each one also declares a contract, callsInPlace(block, EXACTLY_ONCE). That lets the compiler know the block runs exactly once, right now. So you can initialize a val inside the block, and definite-assignment analysis works.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val len: Int = name.let { it.trim().length }          // R = Int
val trimmed: String = name.also { log("raw=$it") }    // T = String (unchanged)
val intent = Intent(ctx, DetailActivity::class.java).apply {
    putExtra("id", id)                                // this = Intent
    addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP)
}
val area = with(rect) { width() * height() }          // not an extension
val ok = prefs.run { getBoolean("onboarded", false) } // this = prefs, returns Boolean

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking apply returns the lambda result. Writing val x = list.apply { size } gives you back the list, not the size.
  • Calling them "keywords" or saying they allocate a lambda. They're inline stdlib functions, so there's no Function object at the call site.
  • Saying with works on nullable objects safely. with(nullable) { } makes this nullable, so you end up writing ?. everywhere. Use nullable?.run { } instead.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which ones can you rename the parameter on? → Only let and also, because they take (T) -> R. this-based ones can only be reached with labels such as this@apply.
  2. Why does val x: Int; run { x = 5 } compile? → Because of the callsInPlace(EXACTLY_ONCE) contract. Without it, the compiler couldn't prove x is assigned once.
  3. Is there a performance difference between them? → No. All are inline, and the bytecode is the same as hand-written code. The only cost is readability.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate recites a table. A senior derives the table from the two signature shapes ((T)->R vs T.()->R, returning T vs R). They mention the contract and inlining, and say the real decision is about what reads clearly to the next person.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Most scope-function bugs in review come from not knowing the return value: an apply used where a transform was meant, or a let that returns Unit or null. See Q128.

questions.promptHtml: apply and also both return the object. When do you pick one over the other?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you choose by intent (configure vs side effect) or at random.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I use apply to configure the object itself. Inside it, this is the object, so property assignments and setter calls read like a builder. I use also for an extra action that isn't part of building the object, like logging, validation, adding it to a list, or assigning it to a field. Because also names the object it, the outer this stays as it was, and that's exactly what you want when the side effect involves the enclosing class.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The object flows through both calls unchanged. The difference is scoping.

  • apply { } puts the object in the innermost implicit receiver slot. Any unqualified name is looked up on the object first, then on outer receivers. That's great for textSize = 14f; setPadding(...). It's dangerous when the object and the enclosing class share member names (see Q127).
  • also { } doesn't change this. it is the object, and this is still your Fragment or ViewModel. That makes it safe for "do this as well", the meaning in its name.

A readable rule: if you can say "build it, and apply these settings", use apply. If you can say "and also, by the way, do X with it", use also.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private fun createRecycler(): RecyclerView =
    RecyclerView(requireContext()).apply {          // configure
        layoutManager = LinearLayoutManager(context)
        adapter = this@ListFragment.adapter          // name clash: must qualify
        setHasFixedSize(true)
    }.also { recycler = it }                         // side effect: keep a reference

fun parse(json: String): Config =
    adapter.fromJson(json)!!.also { require(it.version >= 2) { "old config" } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using also to configure (it.a = 1; it.b = 2). It works, but it's noisy, and it signals the wrong intent.
  • Using apply for logging inside a class. log(this) inside apply logs the object, not the class, which may or may not be what you meant.
  • Expecting changes made inside also to be "undone". Both work on the same instance. also isn't a copy.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can apply be used on a nullable? → x?.apply { } runs only when non-null and returns x (nullable). Without ?., this is nullable inside.
  2. What does also return if the lambda throws? → Nothing. The exception propagates, because inline code behaves like straight-line code.
  3. Why does adapter = adapter inside apply silently do nothing? → Both names resolve to the RecyclerView's own adapter (the innermost receiver), so it assigns the property to itself. Use this@ListFragment.adapter.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate says "apply for objects, also for logging". A senior explains it as receiver shadowing. apply changes name resolution and also doesn't, and that's why also is the safe choice when the side effect touches the enclosing class.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A self-assignment like adapter = adapter inside apply produced an empty list screen that shipped. It passed review because it "looked right".

questions.promptHtml: When would you write x?.let { } instead of if (x != null) { }?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who use ?.let everywhere from people who know why it exists, which is reading a mutable property once.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For a local val or a parameter, if (x != null) is clearer, and smart casts handle it. I reach for ?.let when x is a mutable var property or something the compiler can't smart-cast, such as an open property or a property from another module. ?.let reads the value once into it, which is a stable local, so there's no "smart cast impossible" error and no race between the check and the use. I don't use ?.let { } ?: run { } as an if/else, because the else branch also runs when the let block itself returns null.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Smart cast limits. (Full rules are in the type-system chunk.) For a var class property, if (user != null) user.name fails, because the compiler can't prove another thread or call didn't null it between the check and the use. user?.let { it.name } compiles to "read the field into a temp, null-check the temp, use the temp", so it's correct by construction.
  • Expression vs statement. ?.let is an expression that yields R?. That's useful for val title = item?.let { format(it) }.
  • Chains. a?.b?.let { use(it) } stays flat, where nested ifs would add depth.
  • When if is better. If there's real else logic, use if/else or when. It's honest about both branches, and it avoids the elvis trap.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class PlayerController {
    private var player: ExoPlayerWrapper? = null

    fun pause() {
        // if (player != null) player.pause()   // error: smart cast impossible (mutable property)
        player?.let { it.pause() }              // one read, stable local
        player?.pause()                         // even simpler when it's one call
    }

    fun title(): String {
        val p = player ?: return "Idle"         // capture-then-smart-cast also works
        return p.mediaTitle
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• x?.let { doA(it) } ?: doB(). If doA returns null, doB runs as well (see Q128).
  • Calling player!! inside player?.let { } instead of using it. That re-reads the field and brings the race back (see Q134).
  • Writing ?.let { it.foo() } when ?.foo() is enough.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does ?.let protect against concurrent modification? → It reads once, so it's free of the check-then-use race. But it gives you a snapshot. If another thread changes the property, you're working on the old object.
  2. What's an alternative without let? → val p = player ?: return. Copy to a local and let the smart cast do the rest. It's often the most readable.
  3. Bytecode difference? → let is inline, so it's the same as a temp-variable null check. Zero overhead.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate says "?.let is the Kotlin way to null-check". A senior names the actual reason, a single read of an unstable value. They prefer early return with elvis for readability and call out the ?: run pitfall.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Elvis-after-let showed a fallback UI even when data existed, which is the classic silent bug. Copying a var to a local val fixed a crash cluster where !! came after a null check.

questions.promptHtml: There are two run functions plus with. What's the difference, and when is each one idiomatic?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's a precision check. Many devs don't know that non-extension run exists, or why with is a poor fit for nullables.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: T.run { } is an extension. It makes T the receiver and returns the lambda result, which is good for computing something from an object, especially with ?.run. with(obj) { } does the same thing but takes the object as an argument, so it reads like "with this object, do these things". I use it for non-null objects where I'm calling many members, like a ViewBinding. Plain run { } isn't an extension at all. It's just a block that's also an expression. I use it to group statements where only an expression is allowed, most often after an elvis.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
inline fun <R> run(block: () -> R): R             // no receiver
inline fun <T, R> T.run(block: T.() -> R): R      // extension
inline fun <T, R> with(receiver: T, block: T.() -> R): R
  • T.run and with produce identical bytecode after inlining. The differences are null handling and how they read. x?.run { } short-circuits on null, while with(x) { } has no ?. form.
  • Plain run fits wherever Kotlin wants a single expression: val v = cache[key] ?: run { log("miss"); load(key) }. It also lets you scope temporary locals.
  • with reads best for a "bulk member access" block: with(binding) { title.text = ...; subtitle.text = ... }.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun bind(item: Item) = with(binding) {           // non-null, many member calls
    title.text = item.title
    price.text = item.price.format()
    badge.isVisible = item.isNew
}

val token: String = cachedToken ?: run {         // non-extension run as a block expression
    analytics.log("token_miss")
    refreshToken()
}

val summary = order?.run { "$id: ${items.size} items" } ?: "No order"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• with(maybeNull) { this?.a; this?.b } is ugly. Use ?.run.
  • Using run when you meant apply. val view = TextView(ctx).run { text = "x" } makes view a Unit, so the compiler catches it only if the declared type is explicit.
  • Overusing plain run to "look Kotlin-y" where a private function with a name would be clearer.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you return early from a with block? → return@with value returns from the block. A bare return returns from the enclosing function (non-local return works because it's inline).
  2. Is with(binding) safe in a Fragment after onDestroyView? → It dereferences the binding at the call, so _binding!! would throw there. The scope function changes nothing about lifecycle.
  3. Why does run exist without a receiver? → So you have an inline block expression with a value. Kotlin has no block-expression syntax like { ... } alone, because that would be a lambda.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate treats run and with as synonyms. A senior separates the three signatures, picks ?.run for nullables, with for non-null bulk access, and bare run for elvis blocks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The ?: run { } block after a cache lookup is the most common and legitimate use in data layers. Reviewers should check that the left side can't be null for a "valid" reason.

questions.promptHtml: What do scope functions compile to, and what does that imply for return, performance and allocation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors are expected to reason about cost and control flow, not just syntax. (The general inline mechanics belong to the inline chunk. Here the focus is the scope-function consequences.)

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: They're all inline with callsInPlace(EXACTLY_ONCE) contracts. The compiler pastes the body in at the call site, so there's no lambda object, no virtual call, and no extra stack frame. The apply you see in source simply disappears in bytecode. That has three effects. A bare return inside one returns from the enclosing function. return@let exits only the block. And the compiler knows the block runs exactly once, so val initialization and smart casts after the block work.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Bytecode. x.also { log(it) } becomes roughly val tmp = x; log(tmp); tmp. Decompile with "Show Kotlin Bytecode" and you'll see temp locals like $i$a$-also-Foo$bar$1. There's no Function1 allocation. That holds for K1 and K2 (Kotlin 2.0 uses invokedynamic only for non-inlined lambdas).
  • Non-local return. Because the lambda is inlined, return means "return from the function I'm written in". Inside a ?.let in a ViewModel method, a bare return skips everything after it, including state resets.
  • Labels. return@let value makes value the block's result. this@apply reaches a shadowed receiver.
  • Contracts. EXACTLY_ONCE allows: 
    val config: Config
prefs.run { config = Config(getString("a", "")!!) }   // ok
  • The cost is readability, not CPU. Deep nesting of inlined blocks can bloat a function's bytecode in pathological generated code, but for scope functions that's essentially never a real problem.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun onSave(form: Form?) {
    form?.let {
        if (!it.isValid) return          // non-local: leaves onSave entirely
        repository.save(it)
    }
    _state.update { it.copy(saving = false) }   // skipped when invalid form returned above
}

fun normalized(raw: String?): String =
    raw?.let { s ->
        if (s.isBlank()) return@let "N/A"        // local: exits only the let
        s.trim()
    } ?: "N/A"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a bare return inside let meaning "skip this block". It exits the whole function.
  • Believing that "functional style allocates". Scope functions don't. Collection operators like map do allocate intermediate lists, but that's a different topic.
  • Thinking return@let exists on apply. Every one has its own label: return@apply exists too, but the value is ignored, since apply returns the receiver.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you call a suspend function inside let in a suspend function? → Yes. The inlined body is part of the enclosing suspend function, so suspension works.
  2. Would making these non-inline matter? → Yes. Non-local return would be impossible, there'd be a lambda allocation per call (or an invokedynamic site), and suspend calls inside wouldn't be allowed unless the lambda type were suspend.
  3. How do you verify "no allocation"? → Use Tools > Kotlin > Show Kotlin Bytecode > Decompile and look for the absence of Function1/Lambda classes. Or check the dex in APK Analyzer for generated lambda classes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate says "they're inline so they're fast". A senior connects inlining to control flow (non-local return, labels), to the contracts (val init, once-only), and to suspend-ability. They also say the real cost is readability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A bare return in a ?.let skipped the isLoading = false reset and left the screen on a spinner forever. A unit test asserting the final state would have caught it.

questions.promptHtml: What do takeIf and takeUnless do, and where do they help or hurt?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows command of the stdlib beyond the big five, and awareness of eager evaluation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: x.takeIf { pred(it) } returns x when the predicate is true and null otherwise. takeUnless is the inverse. They turn a condition into nullability, so you can chain ?. and ?: instead of writing if/else. They're good for things like file.takeIf { it.exists() }?.readText(). The catch is that the receiver is always evaluated first, even when the predicate fails, so expensive().takeIf { cheapCheck } still pays for expensive(). And a long chain of takeIf, let and elvis is often worse than a plain if.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
inline fun <T> T.takeIf(predicate: (T) -> Boolean): T?    // contract: callsInPlace(EXACTLY_ONCE)
inline fun <T> T.takeUnless(predicate: (T) -> Boolean): T?
  • Evaluation order. The receiver expression is evaluated, then the predicate runs. There's no short-circuit before the receiver.
  • Return type is T?. Even when T is non-null, so you always deal with nullability downstream.
  • Null-receiver ambiguity. On a nullable receiver, null can mean either "the value was null" or "the predicate failed". If you need to tell them apart, don't use takeIf.
  • Good fits: guarding parsing (s.toIntOrNull()?.takeIf { it in 1..100 }), filtering a single value in a chain, returning null from a finder.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val port = input.toIntOrNull()?.takeIf { it in 1024..65535 } ?: DEFAULT_PORT

val cached = diskCache.read(key)                // I/O always happens
    .takeIf { it != null && !it.isExpired() }   // ok if read() is cheap; else check first

// Hurts: hard to read, and the side effect in the predicate is surprising
val u = repo.user().takeUnless { it.banned.also { b -> if (b) track("ban") } }?.let { map(it) } ?: guest

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Side effects inside the predicate. It runs exactly once, but readers don't expect it.
  • Using takeIf to avoid computing something. It never avoids computing the receiver.
  • Confusing takeIf with filter on collections: list.takeIf { it.isNotEmpty() } returns the whole list or null, not filtered elements.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does takeIf allocate? → No, it's inline. Boxing can still happen if T is a primitive (the generic return T? boxes an Int).
  2. takeIf vs if (c) x else null? → They're semantically equal. Use the if when the condition doesn't depend on x or isn't a simple predicate.
  3. Can it run on a null receiver? → Yes, T can be nullable. The predicate receives null, so you'd generally write x?.takeIf { }.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate knows the definition. A senior points out eager receiver evaluation, the Int boxing via T?, null ambiguity, and the readability break-even with an if.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: api.fetch().takeIf { featureFlag } still hit the network when the flag was off. The intent was to skip the call, so the flag check must come first.

questions.promptHtml: How do you decide which scope function to use, and when do you use none at all?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors set team conventions. Interviewers want a decision rule plus taste, meaning knowing when they hurt.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I ask two questions: do I want the object back or a result, and do I need the outer this kept? That gives me apply or also versus let or run. Then I check whether a plain local val or an if would read better, and it often does. My team rules are: at most one scope function per expression, no nesting this-receiver functions (apply inside with), always name it when nesting, and never use them just to avoid declaring a variable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Decision flow:

Need the object itself back?
 ├─ yes → configuring its members?  → apply
 │        side effect / outer this needed? → also
 └─ no (want a result)
          ├─ object nullable / chaining?   → ?.let (or ?.run when calling many members)
          ├─ non-null, many member calls?  → with
          └─ just need a block expression? → run { }
Then ask: would `val x = ...` + plain code be clearer? If yes, use that.

Readability costs grow non-linearly:

  • Implicit receivers stack. In with(a) { b.apply { foo() } }, foo may resolve to b, a, or the class. The reader has to know all three types.
  • it shadowing. In a nested let, the inner it hides the outer one, and the IDE warns: "Implicit parameter 'it' of enclosing lambda is shadowed".
  • Debugging. Breakpoints and stepping work fine, since the code is inlined, but long chains make logs and stack lines less precise. One line number covers five operations.
  • Diff noise. Converting a chain to add one statement rewrites the whole chain.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Over-chained
fun load(id: String?) = id?.let { repo.find(it) }?.also { cache.put(it.id, it) }
    ?.run { copy(name = name.trim()) }?.let { _state.value = UiState.Ok(it) } ?: run { _state.value = UiState.Missing }

// Clearer
fun load(id: String?) {
    val user = id?.let(repo::find)
    if (user == null) { _state.value = UiState.Missing; return }
    cache.put(user.id, user)
    _state.value = UiState.Ok(user.copy(name = user.name.trim()))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Choosing by habit (let everywhere) instead of by return value and receiver.
  • Nesting two this-receiver functions, which makes name resolution ambiguous to humans.
  • Using also to sneak in state mutations in the middle of a pure-looking chain.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you enforce this? → Code review guidelines, detekt rules (for example NestedScopeFunctions in recent detekt versions, which is configurable; verify the rule name for your detekt version), and IDE inspections for shadowed it.
  2. Do function references help? → id?.let(repo::find) removes a lambda layer and reads as a pipeline.
  3. Is with or apply inside Compose code an issue? → It's fine syntactically, but the same readability rules apply. Compose's own DSL already stacks receivers like Modifier, RowScope and so on.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate knows the table. A senior has a written rule, can name the specific readability failures (receiver stacking, it shadowing, elvis-after-let), and refactors chains to plain code without ego.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The single biggest source of scope-function incidents is not a wrong pick, it's a long chain where one link returns null or Unit unexpectedly (see Q128 and Q130).

questions.promptHtml: What is an extension function, and what does it compile to on the JVM?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Everything else about extensions (static dispatch, no private access, Java call syntax) follows from the compiled form. They want to see you know it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An extension function lets you call receiver.foo() on a type you don't own, without inheritance or wrappers. It doesn't modify the class at all. It compiles to a static method in a facade class named after the file, like StringExtKt, and the receiver becomes the first parameter. So "abc".isEmail() compiles to StringExtKt.isEmail("abc"). That's why extensions can't touch private members, can't be overridden polymorphically, and why Java calls them as static utilities.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Declaration: fun String.isEmail(): Boolean = .... Inside, this is the receiver, called the extension receiver.
  • Compiled form (top-level, in StringExt.kt): 
    public final class StringExtKt {
    public static final boolean isEmail(@NotNull String $this$isEmail) { ... }
}
    The receiver parameter gets a non-null intrinsic check like any public non-null parameter.
  • Consequences:
    • It's resolved at compile time from the declared type of the receiver (Q119).
    • It only sees public API, or internal API in the same module. It can't see private or protected members.
    • Members with the same signature always win (Q120).
    • Java sees StringExtKt.isEmail(s). You can rename the facade with @file:JvmName("StringUtils").
  • Why use them: discoverability through autocomplete on the type, chainable call syntax, and scoping helpers to a file or module.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// StringExt.kt
@file:JvmName("StringUtils")
package com.app.util

fun String.maskEmail(): String {
    val at = indexOf('@')
    return if (at <= 1) this else this[0] + "***" + substring(at)
}

// Kotlin: "jane@x.com".maskEmail()
// Java:   StringUtils.maskEmail("jane@x.com");

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking extensions "inject" methods into the class at runtime. Reflection on String::class won't show them.
  • Expecting to access private fields of the receiver.
  • Forgetting the import. Extensions in other packages need to be imported, otherwise autocomplete suggests them but the code won't compile until imported.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can extensions be generic? → Yes: fun <T> List<T>.second(): T = this[1]. They can also be inline with reified type parameters.
  2. Where can they be declared? → Top-level, as class members (member extensions, Q125), or locally inside a function.
  3. Do they increase method count? → Each one is a static method in the facade class, so they're counted like any method. R8 inlines or removes unused ones.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate says "it adds a function to a class". A senior says "it's a static function with the receiver as its first parameter" and derives the limits (static resolution, no private access, member wins, Java syntax) from that.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams hit Java-interop friction when Java modules have to call FooKt.bar(x). @file:JvmName and a cohesive file per receiver type keep it tidy.

questions.promptHtml: If I declare fun Shape.name() and fun Circle.name(), then call name() on a Shape variable holding a Circle, which one runs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the classic trick question. Getting it wrong shows you think extensions are polymorphic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The Shape one. Extensions are resolved statically at compile time from the declared (static) type of the expression, not the runtime type. The compiler sees Shape, picks Shape.name(), and emits a static call. Overload resolution happens at compile time, and there's no vtable involved. If I need per-subtype behavior, I make it a member (open or abstract), or I write one extension with a when over a sealed type.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• A member call shape.area() compiles to invokevirtual, so the JVM picks the implementation from the runtime class.
  • An extension call compiles to invokestatic ShapeExtKt.name(shape). There are two overloads, name(Shape) and name(Circle). Java-style overload resolution uses the static argument type, so name(Shape) wins.
  • The same applies to smart casts. After if (shape is Circle), the static type is Circle, so Circle.name() is chosen. Static resolution respects whatever the compiler knows at that point.
val s: Shape = Circle()
s.area()   -> invokevirtual Shape.area   -> runtime: Circle.area   (polymorphic)
s.name()   -> invokestatic name(Shape)   -> "Shape"                (static)
if (s is Circle) s.name() -> invokestatic name(Circle) -> "Circle" (smart cast)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface Shape
data class Circle(val r: Double) : Shape
data class Square(val side: Double) : Shape

fun Shape.label() = "shape"
fun Circle.label() = "circle"

fun render(items: List<Shape>) = items.map { it.label() }  // all "shape"

// Fix: single extension dispatching explicitly, exhaustive over the sealed type
fun Shape.displayName(): String = when (this) {
    is Circle -> "circle r=$r"
    is Square -> "square ${side}"
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Building "polymorphism" with extension overloads per subtype, then iterating a List<Base>.
  • Assuming generics change this. fun <T : Shape> T.label() still binds at compile time to the inferred T.
  • Missing that smart casts change the result, so code behaves differently inside and outside an is check.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is there any runtime dispatch in extensions? → Only for the dispatch receiver of a member extension declared open (Q125). The extension receiver itself is always static.
  2. Why didn't Kotlin make them virtual? → They're compiled as static methods outside the class hierarchy. Virtual dispatch would need runtime type checks or class modification.
  3. How would you catch this in review? → Look for the same extension name overloaded on a parent and a child type. That's almost always a smell. Prefer a member or a when over sealed types.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate may guess "Circle". A senior answers "Shape", explains invokestatic vs invokevirtual, mentions the smart-cast nuance, and offers the sealed-when fix.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Per-subtype extension overloads in a ViewHolder renderer made every item in a heterogeneous List<FeedItem> render as the base case (see Q129).

questions.promptHtml: What happens if a class already has a member function with the same name and signature as my extension?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests resolution rules and awareness of upgrade risk.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The member always wins. If the member's signature is applicable, the compiler never picks the extension, and the IDE warns "Extension is shadowed by a member". An extension with a different parameter list is just an overload, and overload resolution picks it normally. The danger is upgrades: if a library adds a member that matches my extension, my call sites silently switch to the library's implementation at the next compile, with no error.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Resolution order (simplified): members of the receiver type come first, then extensions in scope. Among extensions, it goes by scope nesting and import priority (explicit imports beat star imports, which beat default imports such as kotlin.*).
  • Same name, different params: fun Example.print(i: Int) and member print() coexist, and each call is resolved by its arguments.
  • Warning only: shadowing is a warning, not an error. Builds with allWarningsAsErrors would catch it. Many projects don't enable that.
  • Upgrade hazard: it applies to both Java and Kotlin library types. Since the extension is still in the source, nothing breaks visibly. Behavior just changes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Money(val cents: Long) {
    fun format(): String = "%.2f".format(cents / 100.0)        // member
}

fun Money.format(): String = "₹" + cents / 100                 // WARNING: shadowed by member; never called
fun Money.format(locale: java.util.Locale): String =           // fine: different signature, real overload
    java.text.NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(locale).format(cents / 100.0)

Money(1999).format()              // "19.99" (member)
Money(1999).format(Locale.US)     // "$19.99" (extension)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Ignoring the "shadowed" warning because the build is green.
  • Assuming the extension "overrides" the member for your module. It never does.
  • Naming extensions with generic names (toJson, format, isValid) on third-party types, which maximizes collision risk.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a generic member be shadowed by a more specific extension? → No. If the member is applicable, it's chosen even when the extension is more specific.
  2. How do you protect against library upgrades? → Enable warnings-as-errors (at least for EXTENSION_SHADOWED_BY_MEMBER, if your build lets you promote specific warnings), use distinctive names, and run behavior tests on formatting and serialization output.
  3. What about extension vs extension conflicts? → They're resolved by scope and imports. Same priority with no winner gives an ambiguity error, which you fix with an import alias.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate knows "member wins". A senior connects it to dependency upgrades that change behavior silently, and to concrete defenses (naming, warnings-as-errors, golden tests).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An SDK upgrade added a member toJson() that matched a team's extension, and backend payloads changed format overnight (see Q132).

questions.promptHtml: How do extensions on nullable types work, and how does isNullOrEmpty() let the compiler smart-cast afterward?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks understanding of how this can be null, plus awareness of contracts.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Declare the receiver type as nullable, like fun String?.orDash(). Then the call s.orDash() doesn't need ?., and inside the body this may be null, so you handle it yourself. That's how isNullOrEmpty, orEmpty and toString on Any? work. isNullOrEmpty also declares a contract, returns(false) implies (this@isNullOrEmpty != null), so after if (!s.isNullOrEmpty()) the compiler smart-casts s to non-null. Contracts are covered in the DSL chunk. The point here is that a nullable-receiver extension is null-safe by design, while s?.ext() skips the call entirely on null.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• fun T?.ext() called on null really executes, with this == null. Calling s?.ext() on a nullable-receiver extension is legal but redundant, and it changes semantics: the call is skipped and the result is null.
  • The compiled static method takes a nullable parameter, so no null intrinsic check is emitted for the receiver.
  • Design guidance: use nullable receivers for "normalize or inspect" helpers (orEmpty, isNullOrBlank, orZero). Don't use them for "act on" helpers, because null.sendAnalytics() running silently hides bugs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun Int?.orZero(): Int = this ?: 0
fun CharSequence?.isPresent(): Boolean = !isNullOrBlank()   // no contract: no smart cast after use

fun show(name: String?) {
    if (!name.isNullOrEmpty()) {
        println(name.length)        // smart cast via stdlib contract
    }
    if (name.isPresent()) {
        // println(name.length)     // error: our helper has no contract, so no smart cast
        println(name!!.length)
    }
}

val count: Int = response?.items?.size.orZero()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing x?.isNullOrEmpty(). The result becomes Boolean?, and it skips the call on null, which is the opposite of the intent.
  • Writing your own isNullOrX() helpers and expecting smart casts. You only get them with a contract (kotlin.contracts, an opt-in experimental API as of Kotlin 2.x; verify the status for your version).
  • Making action extensions nullable, which hides null bugs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does null.toString() return in Kotlin? → "null", via the stdlib fun Any?.toString() extension.
  2. Can a nullable-receiver extension conflict with a non-null one? → Both can exist. For a non-null static type the more specific T version wins, for nullable the T? one.
  3. Inside a nullable-receiver extension, how do you call members? → After a check: if (this == null) return ...; length. Smart cast works on this.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate knows isNullOrEmpty. A senior explains that this can be null, that ?. on such calls is redundant and changes the semantics, where the smart cast comes from (contracts), and when not to design nullable receivers.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom String?.isValidEmail() without a contract forced !! at every call site. One refactor that removed the check turned the !! into crashes.

questions.promptHtml: Can extension properties have state? How would you attach data to a class you don't own, and what are the risks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors are expected to know the hard limit (no backing field) and the leak and perf traps in the common workarounds.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: No. Extension properties have no backing field, because they compile to static getter and setter methods and there's nowhere in the object to store state. So initializers aren't allowed, and each access recomputes in the getter. To attach data, you either use storage the type already provides, like View.setTag(key, value), or an external map. An external map has to use weak keys, or it leaks every object you ever touched. Even then, an identity-based weak map on Android is easy to get wrong. Often the right answer is a wrapper class or a member on a type you do own.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• val String.wordCount: Int get() = split(" ").size compiles to static int getWordCount(String). It's computed on each access, and there's no caching. An expensive getter in a hot path (RecyclerView bind, Compose recomposition) is hidden work, because it looks like a field read.
  • var House.number = 1 is a compile error: "Initializers are not allowed for extension properties".
  • Ways to attach state:
Approach Leak risk Notes
View.setTag(R.id.key, v) Tied to the View's lifetime The Android-blessed way. AndroidX uses this pattern internally.
HashMap<Obj, V> global Every key is strongly held forever Leaks Activities and Views.
WeakHashMap<Obj, V> Keys are weak, but a value referencing its key keeps it alive Uses equals/hashCode, not identity. Mutable keys break lookups.
Wrapper or composition None The most explicit, at the cost of a wrapper type.
  • WeakHashMap is not thread-safe. Wrap it or confine it to the main thread.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// OK: state lives in the View itself
var View.trackingId: String?
    get() = getTag(R.id.tracking_id) as? String
    set(value) = setTag(R.id.tracking_id, value)

// Leak: Activity keys held forever
private val screenNames = HashMap<Activity, String>()
var Activity.screenName: String
    get() = screenNames[this] ?: javaClass.simpleName
    set(v) { screenNames[this] = v }

// Hidden cost: looks like a field, allocates a formatter on every access
val Context.dateFormatter: java.text.DateFormat
    get() = java.text.DateFormat.getDateInstance(java.text.DateFormat.MEDIUM, resources.configuration.locales[0])

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a global strong map for "extension state", which leaks every key.
  • A WeakHashMap whose value holds a reference to its key (for example a listener capturing the View), so the key never clears.
  • Expensive getters that read like fields, called in loops.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why doesn't Kotlin allow by lazy on extension properties? → A delegate needs a field to store the delegate instance per object, and extensions have none. A top-level by lazy is a single shared value, not per receiver.
  2. Is a computed extension property ever better than a function? → Yes, when it's cheap, has no side effects, and is conceptually an attribute (val Int.dp). Anything that does I/O or allocates should be a function, so the call looks like work.
  3. Thread-safety of a setTag approach? → Views are main-thread-only anyway, so it's confined by convention.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate knows "no backing field". A senior covers the recomputation cost, leak-proof storage (setTag), the WeakHashMap value-references-key trap, thread-safety, and when to prefer a wrapper.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A HashMap<Activity, ...> behind an extension property was a top LeakCanary signature, retaining about 3 Activities per rotation. See Q131 for the perf variant.

questions.promptHtml: How do visibility modifiers and imports work for extensions? How do you resolve two libraries defining the same extension?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors design module APIs. Leaking helper extensions across modules pollutes autocomplete and creates coupling.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Extensions follow normal visibility. A private top-level extension is visible only in that file, internal only in the module, and public everywhere it's imported. An extension can only see what its scope can see. It can't touch the receiver's private or protected members, but a top-level extension can use private declarations in its own file. Callers in other packages must import it by name or with a star import. If two libraries clash, I import one with an alias, like import com.lib.a.toUiModel as toUiModelA, or call it in fully qualified form.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Default visibility is public. Every helper extension in a shared module becomes part of its API, and shows up in autocomplete for every consumer on very common types like String, Context and View.
  • Use internal for module-private helpers, and private for file-local ones. Kotlin's explicit API mode (kotlin { explicitApi() }) forces you to state visibility on public declarations, which is good for library modules.
  • Imports: the extension's package must be imported. import com.app.ext.* imports all top-level declarations in the package. Same-package declarations need no import.
  • Clashes: with two applicable extensions of the same priority, the compiler reports ambiguity. Fix it with an alias import (as), a narrower import, or by moving one to a different scope.
  • Java view: internal declarations compile to public bytecode with mangled names for members. Top-level internal functions are public static in the facade. Java code can call them, so internal isn't a security boundary.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :feature:checkout, PriceExt.kt
package com.app.checkout

private val inr = java.text.NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(java.util.Locale("en", "IN"))

internal fun Long.toRupees(): String = inr.format(this / 100.0)   // module-only, uses private file val

// Consumer resolving a name clash
import com.vendor.analytics.toEvent as toVendorEvent
import com.app.tracking.toEvent

fun track(click: Click) { send(click.toEvent()); vendor.send(click.toVendorEvent()) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaving everything public in a :core:ui module, so 300 extensions on Context flood autocomplete in every feature.
  • Believing internal hides code from Java or reflection.
  • Expecting protected on top-level declarations. It's not allowed there.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a private extension in a class be used outside the class? → No. A member extension marked private is only usable inside that class.
  2. Does @file:JvmName change Kotlin import paths? → No. Kotlin imports by package plus name, and the JvmName only affects the JVM facade class name.
  3. How would you audit public extension surface? → Use the binary-compatibility-validator plugin (apiDump and apiCheck) or explicit API mode in library modules.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate knows the modifiers. A senior talks about API surface hygiene (explicit API, internal by default), clash resolution with aliases, and that internal is a compile-time, not runtime, boundary.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Two modules each defined fun Context.toast(...) with different durations. Whichever import the IDE auto-added won, and the UX was inconsistent across screens (see Q133).

questions.promptHtml: How do you write a "static-like" extension, like Intent.Companion.forDetail(...)? When does that work and when doesn't it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks knowledge of companion extensions and their limit: you can't add static members to Java classes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If a Kotlin class has a companion object, I can extend it with fun MyClass.Companion.create(...), and callers write MyClass.create(...) as if it were static. Kotlin's companion is a real object instance, so the extension is just an extension on that object's type. The limit is that it only works when a companion exists. I can't add one to a Kotlin class I don't own that lacks one, and Java classes like Intent or String have no companion at all, so Intent.Companion doesn't exist. Then the options are a top-level factory function or an object holding factories.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The companion compiles to a nested class Foo.Companion with a static Companion field instance. fun Foo.Companion.bar() compiles to a static method taking Foo.Companion as its receiver. A call Foo.bar() loads Foo.Companion and passes it.
  • You can add a companion only to your own class. Even an empty companion object exists to make extensions possible, which is a common library trick (for example kotlin.String.Companion exists in the stdlib, so String.Companion extensions are legal).
  • Java callers: FooKt.bar(Foo.Companion), which is awkward. @JvmStatic doesn't apply to extensions declared outside the companion.
  • Alternatives for Java types: top-level fun detailIntent(ctx, id): Intent, or fun Context.detailIntent(id). The receiver extension on Context is often the most discoverable.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class UserId(val raw: String) {
    companion object                                   // empty, intentionally extensible
}

fun UserId.Companion.parse(s: String): UserId? =
    s.takeIf { it.matches(Regex("u_[0-9a-f]{8}")) }?.let(::UserId)

val id = UserId.parse("u_1a2b3c4d")

// Java type: no companion, so use a receiver extension or top-level factory
fun Context.detailIntent(id: UserId): Intent =
    Intent(this, DetailActivity::class.java).putExtra("id", id.raw)

// fun Intent.Companion.forDetail() {}   // error: Intent has no companion

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming Intent.Companion exists because Kotlin classes have companions. Java classes don't.
  • Forgetting that removing an "empty" companion from a library class breaks all downstream companion extensions. That's an ABI and source break.
  • Confusing a companion extension with @JvmStatic members. Only members declared inside the companion can be @JvmStatic.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does String.Companion exist? → Yes, the stdlib declares it, so fun String.Companion.randomId() works as String.randomId(). Verify for other stdlib types before relying on it.
  2. Can a companion extension access private members of the companion? → No. Same rule as all extensions.
  3. Why might a library ship an empty companion? → So consumers (or the library's own other modules) can add Type.factory()-style extensions, which keeps the class API small.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate may not know companion extensions exist. A senior explains the mechanics, the Java-class limit, the library design trick of empty companions, and the API-compat implications.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team removed a "useless" empty companion from a shared model class, and three feature modules failed to compile on Model.fromDto(...) extensions.

questions.subtopic: Member extensions, dispatch vs extension receiver
questions.promptHtml: What's a member extension? Explain dispatch receiver vs extension receiver, and which of them is virtual.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's a senior-level resolution question. It underpins DSLs, scoped helpers, and subtle name-resolution bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A member extension is an extension declared inside a class, like class Formatter { fun Money.display() = ... }. It has two implicit receivers: the extension receiver (Money) and the dispatch receiver (the Formatter instance). It's only callable where a Formatter is in scope, inside the class or in with(formatter) { }. If you mark it open and override it, dispatch is virtual on the dispatch receiver, chosen by the runtime Formatter subclass. It's still static on the extension receiver, chosen by the declared type of Money. When names clash, the extension receiver's members win, and you reach the outer one with this@Formatter.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Compiled form: an instance method on the dispatch class, with the extension receiver as its first parameter: Formatter.display(Money). Calling it uses invokevirtual on the Formatter. That's where the virtual part comes from.
  • Resolution inside the body: unqualified names are looked up on the extension receiver first, then the dispatch receiver, then outer scopes. That's the source of shadowing bugs (Q135).
  • Scoping power: this is how DSLs restrict where helpers are callable, for example RowScope.weight() in Compose. Modifier.weight is a member extension of RowScope, so it only resolves inside a Row lambda. Coroutines' CoroutineScope-receiver builders follow the same idea.
open class A; class B : A()
open class Base {
    open fun A.f() = "Base on A"
    open fun B.f() = "Base on B"
    fun call(a: A) = a.f()          // a's declared type is A, so A.f is chosen at compile time
}
class Derived : Base() {
    override fun A.f() = "Derived on A"
    override fun B.f() = "Derived on B"
}

Base().call(B())     -> "Base on A"     (static on extension receiver A)
Derived().call(B())  -> "Derived on A"  (virtual on dispatch receiver Base/Derived)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
open class PriceRenderer {
    open fun Long.asPrice(): String = "₹" + this / 100
    fun render(cents: Long) = cents.asPrice()
}

class UsPriceRenderer : PriceRenderer() {
    override fun Long.asPrice(): String = "$" + this / 100
}

val r: PriceRenderer = UsPriceRenderer()
r.render(1999)                         // "$19": virtual on dispatch receiver
with(r) { 500L.asPrice() }             // "$5": callable here because r is an implicit receiver

class Screen(val name: String) {
    fun String.tagged() = "[${this@Screen.name}] $this"   // explicit outer receiver
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting member extensions to be callable like normal extensions from outside the class. They need the dispatch receiver in scope.
  • Forgetting that unqualified names resolve on the extension receiver first (tag, id, context, name).
  • Expecting the extension receiver to be virtual. It never is.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does Modifier.weight() fail outside a Row? → It's a member extension of RowScope. Without a RowScope receiver in scope there's no dispatch receiver, so it doesn't resolve.
  2. Can member extensions be in interfaces? → Yes, including abstract ones. Implementations provide the body, and that's the scope-interface pattern Compose uses.
  3. How do @DslMarker annotations relate? → They restrict implicit access to outer receivers of the same DSL. The details are in the DSL chunk.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate rarely knows the term. A senior explains the two receivers, virtual vs static, name-resolution precedence, this@Outer, and links it to real APIs like RowScope and scope-restricted helpers.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Member extensions in a base Fragment resolved tag on the View instead of the Fragment, and analytics recorded wrong screen names for weeks (Q135).

questions.promptHtml: When should something be an extension vs a member vs a plain top-level function? How do you design extensions for a large codebase?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors make API calls that last for years. The interviewer is checking for taste, plus awareness of discoverability, coupling, testability, and Java interop.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I make something a member when it's core to the type, needs private state, or needs polymorphism. I use an extension when I don't own the type, or when the function is a convenience that belongs to a specific layer, like Dto.toDomain() in the data module, so the domain class stays clean of mapping concerns. I use a plain function when there's no natural "subject" object or there are two equal subjects. For a big codebase: scope extensions to the layer that needs them, keep them internal by default, avoid extending ultra-common types like String, Any and Context with domain logic, and make sure every extension is a pure function of its receiver plus its arguments, so it's trivially testable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Member vs extension trade-offs:
Criterion Member Extension
Access to private state Yes No
Polymorphism Yes (open/override) No (static, Q119)
Works on types you don't own No Yes
Keeps type dependency-free No (pulls in mapping/UI deps) Yes (declared in the layer that needs it)
Mockable Via interface Not directly (static), so test the function itself
Shadowing risk n/a A member added later wins silently (Q120)
  • Layering pattern: fun UserDto.toDomain(): User lives in :data, and fun User.toUi(res: Resources): UserUi lives in :feature. The User type doesn't know about DTOs or Android, so dependency direction is preserved.
  • Testability: since extensions are static, callers can't swap them. Keep anything with side effects (I/O, analytics, time) out of extensions, or inject the collaborator as a parameter or a dispatch receiver.
  • Java interop: Java consumers call FileKt.ext(receiver). If a module is consumed from Java, group extensions per receiver type and set @file:JvmName.
  • Naming: avoid generic verbs on third-party types (format, toJson, isValid), since they risk member collisions (Q132). Prefer intent-revealing names.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :data module: mapping lives with the DTO's layer
internal fun UserDto.toDomain(): User = User(id = UserId(id), name = name.orEmpty().trim())

// Side-effect hidden in an extension: hard to test, hard to see
fun User.markSeen() { Analytics.track("seen", id.raw); Prefs.set("seen_${id.raw}", true) }

// Better: collaborator explicit
class SeenTracker(private val analytics: Analytics, private val prefs: Prefs) {
    fun markSeen(user: User) { analytics.track("seen", user.id.raw); prefs.set("seen_${user.id.raw}", true) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Extensions with hidden singletons or side effects that can't be faked in tests.
  • Domain logic on String ("123".toOrderStatus()) that shows up everywhere in autocomplete.
  • Extensions on a type you do own, used to work around a design you should fix (for example to fake polymorphism).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you mock an extension in tests? → Ideally you don't, because it should be pure. MockK can mock top-level and extension functions with mockkStatic("com.app.FileKt"), but needing that is a design smell.
  2. Should mapper extensions or mapper classes be used? → Extensions for pure 1:1 mapping. Inject a mapper class when mapping needs dependencies (Resources, a clock, feature flags).
  3. Do extensions affect build times or modularity? → Indirectly. A giant :core:ext module that everyone depends on recompiles widely on each change, so split it by domain.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE candidate says "extensions for convenience". A senior gives a decision table, explains layering via extensions, testability and side effects, and collision-safe naming, and treats public extension surface as API.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Moving toUi() extensions out of :core:model into the feature modules removed an Android dependency from the domain layer and cut incremental rebuild fan-out.

questions.contextHtml:
A profile screen sends an update request. QA reports that after editing, the server receives the request but the user's displayed name never changes, and support sees about 1.2% of "profile update" tickets mentioning "my name reverts". There are no crashes, and the backend logs show requests arriving with name equal to the old name. The code passed review:

class EditProfileViewModel(private val api: ProfileApi) : ViewModel() {
    var name: String = ""          // bound to the text field
    var bio: String = ""

    fun save(current: Profile) {
        val request = UpdateRequest(current.id).apply {
            name = name            // intent: copy VM's edited name
            bio = bio
            avatarUrl = current.avatarUrl
        }
        viewModelScope.launch { api.update(request) }
    }
}
class UpdateRequest(val id: String) { var name: String = ""; var bio: String = ""; var avatarUrl: String? = null }

A red herring: the team recently upgraded Retrofit, and someone suspects serialization.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain exactly why it happens, and fix it so it can't come back.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Probably Retrofit or Gson is dropping the field, let's add logging to the interceptor." Or "use also instead" without explaining resolution. That misses that the request object is wrong before it ever reaches Retrofit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the name in the request blank, or the old value? (If it's old, UpdateRequest must default to something else. Here it'd be blank, so I'd check whether the backend treats blank as "no change", which would explain the "reverts" symptom.) Did this code change recently? Are there tests asserting the request body?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the assignments, since it's a one-line change per field. No server change is needed. Verify on an internal build with the request body logged.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Receiver shadowing in apply: name = name resolves both sides to UpdateRequest.name. Highest, because it's visible in the code. (b) Serialization dropping fields after the Retrofit upgrade, which is unlikely since avatarUrl arrives fine. (c) The backend ignores blank fields. That's a contributing explanation for "reverts" rather than "blanks".
  4. How I'd verify each: A unit test on save with a fake API captures the UpdateRequest, and I assert name. An OkHttp HttpLoggingInterceptor in a debug build shows the JSON body. The IDE also flags it: "Variable 'name' is assigned to itself" is a self-assignment inspection.
  5. Root cause: Inside apply, this is the UpdateRequest, the innermost implicit receiver. Unqualified name on both sides resolves to this.name (the request), so it assigns the request's empty default to itself. The ViewModel's name is shadowed. The backend treats an empty name as "unchanged", so the user sees the old name.
  6. Fix: 
    // short-term: qualify the outer receiver
val request = UpdateRequest(current.id).apply {
    name = this@EditProfileViewModel.name
    bio = this@EditProfileViewModel.bio
    avatarUrl = current.avatarUrl
}
// long-term: immutable request, no scope function needed
data class UpdateRequest(val id: String, val name: String, val bio: String, val avatarUrl: String?)
val request = UpdateRequest(current.id, name = name, bio = bio, avatarUrl = current.avatarUrl)
    Named constructor args make the source of every value explicit, and vals prevent post-construction mutation.
  7. Prevention: Treat "assigned to itself" as an error (detekt or IDE inspection severity). Have a code-review rule: no apply when the receiver and the enclosing class share property names. Add a ViewModel test asserting the outgoing request.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't switch blindly to also { it.name = name }. It works, but it hides the real lesson. The immutable data class is the robust fix. I wouldn't chase the Retrofit upgrade without evidence.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if UpdateRequest.name were a val? → Then name = name wouldn't compile (val can't be reassigned). Immutability turns this bug into a compile error.
  • Would with(request) { name = name } behave the same? → Yes. Any this-receiver scope function shadows the same way.
  • How would K2 treat this? → Resolution rules are the same. The self-assignment warning still fires.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A settings sync used Config().apply { timeout = timeout } and every client sent the default 30 s for two releases. A one-line test asserting the outgoing config would have cost five minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames serialization or the network, and can't explain why the value is wrong.
  • Hire: Spots the shadowing and fixes it with this@... or also.
  • Strong hire: Explains implicit receiver precedence, links the "reverts" symptom to backend blank handling, proposes immutable requests plus inspection/test prevention, and dismisses the Retrofit red herring with evidence.

questions.contextHtml:
After release 4.12 (rolled out to 50% of 2M DAU), product sees "login screen shown to already-logged-in users" rise from 0.1% to 3.4% of app opens. There are no crashes. The analytics funnel shows those users tap "login", and auto-login succeeds instantly. The change in 4.12 was a "cleanup" of the splash router:

fun route(session: Session?) {
    session?.let { s ->
        prefetcher.warmUp(s.userId)      // new in 4.12: returns Job? (null if prefetch disabled by flag)
    } ?: navigator.toLogin()
    session?.let { navigator.toHome(it) }
}

prefetcher.warmUp returns null when the remote flag prefetch_enabled is off, and it's off for 70% of the rollout cohort. One more detail: the navigator ignores a second navigation within 300 ms on some devices, which is why only some users see it.
questions.promptHtml: What's going on, and how do you fix it and keep it from coming back?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Session must be expiring, check token refresh," or "a race in the navigator, add a debounce." Both chase red herrings. The bug is that the elvis fires when let returns null.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the spike correlate with the prefetch_enabled flag cohort? (It points to the new call.) Is session actually non-null for these users? (Auto-login succeeding says yes.) What exactly changed in the router diff? Is the navigator's double-navigation handling device-dependent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Flip prefetch_enabled on for everyone (if prefetch is safe), which makes warmUp return non-null, or halt the rollout at 50%. The flag flip is instant, needs no release, and confirms the hypothesis at the same time.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) ?.let { } ?: x fires x when the let block returns null. Strongest, because it correlates with the flag. (b) Session expiry, which contradicts the instant auto-login. (c) A navigator race. It's real, but it's the reason the symptom varies, not the cause.
  4. How I'd verify each: Slice the metric by flag value in analytics. Write a unit test with a non-null session and warmUp returning null, then assert toLogin is never called. Add a temporary breadcrumb log ("toLogin from route, session!=null") to Crashlytics custom logs.
  5. Root cause: a?.let { block } ?: b evaluates b whenever the whole left expression is null. That happens when a is null or when block returns null. The cleanup made the let block's last expression warmUp(...), which returns Job?. With the flag off it returns null, so toLogin() runs even with a valid session. Then toHome runs too. Depending on the navigator's 300 ms de-dupe and device timing, the user ends up on Login or sees a flicker.
  6. Fix: 
    fun route(session: Session?) {
    if (session == null) { navigator.toLogin(); return }
    prefetcher.warmUp(session.userId)
    navigator.toHome(session)
}
    Long-term: make the router a pure function, fun destination(session: Session?): Destination returning a sealed type. Then navigation happens once, in one place.
  7. Prevention: Add a review-checklist and lint rule against ?.let { ... } ?: where the let body's type is nullable or Unit-returning. Detekt has rules around this area for some versions; otherwise write a custom rule. Add tests for router branches with each flag value. Alert on the "login shown with valid session" ratio.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't add ?: Unit or .let { warmUp(); Unit } hacks to "make let non-null". They're fragile, and the next edit breaks them again. I wouldn't add a navigator debounce, which masks the double navigation without fixing the logic.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would session?.also { warmUp(it) } ?: toLogin() be correct? → Yes, because also returns the receiver, which is non-null here. But if/else is still clearer, and safer against future edits.
  • Why didn't the compiler warn? → Job? elvis'd with Unit is type-correct. Nothing is wrong at the type level.
  • How would you detect it if the flag hadn't correlated? → Funnel dashboards per release, plus breadcrumb logs on unexpected branches ("login with valid session").

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cart screen used cart?.let { render(it) } ?: showEmpty(). Months later render began returning a nullable diff result, and full carts flashed "Your cart is empty". It was the same construct with a different team.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Chases tokens or navigation races, and doesn't know the elvis/let semantics.
  • Hire: Identifies that the let block returning null triggers the elvis, and rewrites it with if/else.
  • Strong hire: Uses the flag correlation for diagnosis and mitigation, explains the varying symptom (navigator timing), refactors to a pure destination function, and adds lint/test/metric prevention.

questions.contextHtml:
You're running a post-incident review. A feed with 6 item types (FeedItem sealed interface: Post, Ad, Story, Poll, Video, Event) shipped a "content descriptions for accessibility" change. A week later, TalkBack users report every item is announced as "Feed item" (the generic text). Ad compliance also flags that ads aren't announced as "Sponsored", which is a legal requirement in some markets. The change:

fun FeedItem.a11yLabel(): String = "Feed item"
fun Ad.a11yLabel(): String = "Sponsored: $advertiser"
fun Post.a11yLabel(): String = "Post by $author"
// ... one per subtype

class FeedAdapter : ListAdapter<FeedItem, FeedVH>(Diff) {
    override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: FeedVH, position: Int) {
        val item = getItem(position)                 // static type: FeedItem
        holder.itemView.contentDescription = item.a11yLabel()
        holder.bind(item)
    }
}

Unit tests passed. They called Ad(...).a11yLabel() directly. Screenshot tests passed because they don't check content descriptions. A red herring: the same release bumped RecyclerView, and one engineer believes view recycling reuses stale descriptions.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the review. What's the root cause, why did tests miss it, and what do we change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "RecyclerView is recycling views, so reset contentDescription in onViewRecycled." That treats a symptom that doesn't exist. Every item is wrong, not just recycled ones.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it every item, or only recycled ones? ("Every item, including the first screen", which rules out recycling.) Which markets have the sponsored-label requirement, and since when are we non-compliant? Do we have accessibility checks in CI?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix release. Since ads' legal labelling is affected, consider a server-side fallback (inject "Sponsored" into the advertiser field) to cover users who don't update. Notify legal/compliance with the exposure window.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Extension overloads resolved statically on FeedItem. Fits "every item generic". (b) Recycling stale descriptions. That would show mixed labels, not uniformly generic ones. (c) TalkBack reading a child view instead of the root, which would give different text, not "Feed item".
  4. How I'd verify each: Decompile onBindViewHolder (Show Kotlin Bytecode) and see invokestatic FeedA11yKt.a11yLabel(LFeedItem;). An instrumented test binds an Ad through the adapter and asserts contentDescription. Run Layout Inspector on a device to check the attribute values directly.
  5. Root cause: Extensions are resolved at compile time from the declared type. getItem() returns FeedItem, so the compiler binds to FeedItem.a11yLabel() regardless of the runtime subtype. The unit tests used the concrete static type Ad, so they exercised a different overload than production. The test and the production code took different compile-time paths.
  6. Fix: 
    // Single entry point, exhaustive over the sealed type: adding a subtype forces a compile error
fun FeedItem.a11yLabel(): String = when (this) {
    is Ad    -> "Sponsored: $advertiser"
    is Post  -> "Post by $author"
    is Story -> "Story from $owner"
    is Poll  -> "Poll: $question"
    is Video -> "Video: $title"
    is Event -> "Event: $name"
}
    An alternative is an abstract member val a11yLabel: String on the sealed interface, if UI strings are allowed in the model layer. Usually they aren't, so the when in the UI layer wins. Longer term, use string resources, not hard-coded English.
  7. Prevention: Test through the same static type as production (val item: FeedItem = Ad(...)). Add Espresso accessibility checks (AccessibilityChecks.enable()) plus a content-description assertion per item type. Add a lint or review rule: no extension overloads across a sealed hierarchy. Add a compliance test asserting "Sponsored" on ads.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No is-casting at each call site, which scatters the logic. No reflection or ::class maps. And I wouldn't blame the RecyclerView bump in the write-up without evidence. Blameless reviews still need accurate causes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would generics fix it, like fun <T : FeedItem> T.a11yLabel()? → No. It's still compile-time, and T is inferred as FeedItem.
  • What if the call were inside when (item) { is Ad -> item.a11yLabel() }? → The smart cast makes the static type Ad, so the right overload is picked. That explains why some code paths "worked".
  • How do you make adding a 7th type safe? → The exhaustive when over a sealed interface with no else gives a compile error on new subtypes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payments module had fun Method.fee() overloads per method type, and a List<Method> summary showed the base fee for everything. Finance caught it in reconciliation, not QA.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Accepts the recycling theory, and doesn't know extensions are static.
  • Hire: Identifies static dispatch and fixes it with a sealed when.
  • Strong hire: Explains why the tests passed (different static types), handles compliance urgency, adds accessibility and test-through-supertype prevention, and rules out the red herring with evidence.

questions.contextHtml:
You're reviewing a PR in a repository class that serves an offline-first article reader (800k MAU). The author is proud of "zero local variables":

suspend fun article(id: String): Article? =
    id.takeIf { it.isNotBlank() }
        ?.let { dao.find(it) }
        ?.takeUnless { it.isStale(clock.now()) }
        ?.also { analytics.cacheHit(it.id) }
        ?: id.takeIf { it.isNotBlank() }
            ?.let { api.fetch(it) }
            ?.run { copy(body = body.sanitize()) }
            ?.also { dao.upsert(it) }
            ?.also { analytics.cacheMiss(it.id) }

Facts: api.fetch throws on network errors; dao.find returns Article?. Product reports that stale articles are shown offline about 0% of the time, and users see "Not found" when offline with a stale cache. That's a 2.1% complaint rate on the offline-reading NPS survey. Another reviewer approved it, saying "very idiomatic".
questions.promptHtml: Review this. What's wrong functionally, what's wrong for maintainability, and what would you ask the author to write instead?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks idiomatic, maybe rename it." Or style-only feedback that misses the functional bug.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What's the desired offline behavior? (Serve stale over nothing, I'd assume.) Should a network error throw, or fall back? Does analytics want a "stale served" event?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Don't merge it as is. If an earlier version is already in prod, add a stale fallback quickly behind a flag.
  3. Hypotheses (issues), ranked: (a) Functional: a stale cached article is discarded by takeUnless. Offline, api.fetch throws, so the user gets an exception or "Not found" even though a stale copy existed. The chain structure made "stale but usable" impossible to express. (b) Duplicated validation: takeIf { isNotBlank() } is evaluated twice, and blank ids return null silently instead of failing fast. (c) Hidden side effects: upsert and analytics hide inside alsos in an expression-bodied function. A reader sees a "query", not writes. (d) Debuggability: one expression over ten lines makes stack traces and breakpoints coarse, and the bodies are all it.
  4. How I'd verify each: Write a repository test with a fake DAO holding a stale article and a fake API throwing IOException, then assert the stale article is returned. Add a test for a blank id. Run those tests against the PR to show they fail.
  5. Root cause: The chain encodes a three-way decision (fresh / stale / missing) plus error handling as a sequence of null-propagating steps. Null conflates "missing", "stale" and "invalid input", so the stale branch got lost. That's an expressiveness problem, not a style one.
  6. Fix: 
    suspend fun article(id: String): Article? {
    require(id.isNotBlank()) { "blank article id" }
    val cached = dao.find(id)
    if (cached != null && !cached.isStale(clock.now())) {
        analytics.cacheHit(id); return cached
    }
    return try {
        val fresh = api.fetch(id).let { it.copy(body = it.body.sanitize()) }
        dao.upsert(fresh)
        analytics.cacheMiss(id)
        fresh
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        cached?.also { analytics.staleServed(id) }   // stale beats nothing
    }
}
    (Error-handling policy and cancellation details belong to the coroutine chunks. IOException is narrow enough not to swallow CancellationException.)
  7. Prevention: Team guideline: at most one or two scope functions per expression, no side-effecting also in expression-bodied "getter-like" functions, and branches with distinct business meaning get explicit if/when. Turn on detekt complexity rules for chained scope functions if available. Write tests per branch (fresh, stale+offline, missing+offline, blank).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't ban scope functions. One let for the sanitize mapping is fine. I wouldn't argue taste alone in review. Leading with the failing stale-offline test makes it objective.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should this return a sealed ArticleResult (Fresh/Stale/Missing) instead of Article?? → Often yes. It lets the UI show a "you're offline, showing saved copy" banner. Model design is covered in the generics/sealed chunks.
  • Is the chain faster? → No. Everything is inline, so the bytecode is equivalent. Performance is not an argument either way.
  • The author says "it's functional style". → Functional style favors pure expressions. This chain has three side effects and hidden control flow.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's "no locals" style guide produced 15-line chains. The incident review found three bugs, all at null-conflation points. The guide was rewritten around "explicit branches for business decisions".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Style nitpicks only, or approves.
  • Hire: Finds the stale-discard bug and proposes an if-based rewrite.
  • Strong hire: Frames null conflation as the root cause, makes the review objective with failing tests, separates side effects, addresses offline UX, and proposes durable team guidelines without dogma.

questions.contextHtml:
A transactions list (RecyclerView, typical 2,000 rows, fling-heavy) on low-end devices (2 GB RAM, about 35% of users) shows jank. Android vitals report slow frames at 18% on those devices vs 4% on high-end.
