A Perfetto trace shows onBindViewHolder at p95 = 6.8 ms (budget about 16 ms per frame at 60 Hz, shared with layout and draw), with frequent GC pauses. LeakCanary separately reports TransactionsActivity retained after rotation. Relevant code:

val Context.dateFmt: java.text.DateFormat
    get() = java.text.SimpleDateFormat("dd MMM yyyy, HH:mm", resources.configuration.locales[0])

val Long.asMoney: String
    get() = java.text.NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(java.util.Locale("en", "IN")).format(this / 100.0)

private val rowColors = HashMap<Context, Int>()
var Context.rowColor: Int
    get() = rowColors.getOrPut(this) { ContextCompat.getColor(this, R.color.row) }
    set(v) { rowColors[this] = v }

override fun onBindViewHolder(h: VH, pos: Int) {
    val t = getItem(pos); val ctx = h.itemView.context
    h.date.text = ctx.dateFmt.format(java.util.Date(t.timestamp))
    h.amount.text = t.cents.asMoney
    h.itemView.setBackgroundColor(ctx.rowColor)
}

A red herring: the team's image loader was recently upgraded and someone wants to profile it first. There are no images in this list.
questions.promptHtml: Find the problems, quantify them, and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use DiffUtil and setHasFixedSize," or "profile the image loader". These are generic RecyclerView tips that ignore the hidden allocations behind property syntax, and the leak.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What's the bind rate during a fling? (About 60 to 120 binds/s.) Does the locale change at runtime? (It affects formatter caching.) Are lists ever shown in multiple Activities simultaneously? Is formatting needed per bind, or could it happen once per item?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cache the formatters (low risk, ships next release) and fix the leaking map. No feature flag is needed. These are behavior-preserving changes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Extension property getters allocate a SimpleDateFormat and a NumberFormat on every access. Both are heavyweight objects, since they parse a pattern and load locale data, which causes GC churn. (b) The HashMap<Context, Int> strongly holds every Activity used as a key, which is the leak. (c) The image loader, ruled out because there are no images.
  4. How I'd verify each: Use the Android Studio Memory Profiler allocation tracking during a fling and sort by class (SimpleDateFormat, DecimalFormat, char[]). Add Perfetto slices with trace("bind") { } around formatting. Use LeakCanary's leak trace to see rowColors → HashMap → TransactionsActivity. Write a microbenchmark (Jetpack Microbenchmark) for format-per-call vs cached.
  5. Root cause: Extension properties have no backing field. A val extension with a getter is a function that runs on every read, and here the getters construct formatters. Each bind does 2 formatter constructions plus their internal objects. At about 100 binds/s, that's 200 formatter allocations per second plus garbage, which drives GC on 2 GB devices. The rowColor "cache" is a global strong map keyed by Context, so every rotation leaks the old Activity (about 1 per rotation, with its whole view tree).
  6. Fix: 
    class TransactionFormatter(locale: java.util.Locale) {          // one per adapter, main-thread only
    private val date = java.text.SimpleDateFormat("dd MMM yyyy, HH:mm", locale)
    private val money = java.text.NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(java.util.Locale("en", "IN"))
    fun date(ts: Long): String = date.format(java.util.Date(ts))
    fun money(cents: Long): String = money.format(cents / 100.0)
}

class TxAdapter(context: Context) : ListAdapter<Tx, VH>(Diff) {
    private val fmt = TransactionFormatter(context.resources.configuration.locales[0])
    private val rowColor = ContextCompat.getColor(context, R.color.row)   // resolved once, no global map
    override fun onBindViewHolder(h: VH, pos: Int) {
        val t = getItem(pos)
        h.date.text = fmt.date(t.timestamp)
        h.amount.text = fmt.money(t.cents)
        h.itemView.setBackgroundColor(rowColor)
    }
}
    SimpleDateFormat isn't thread-safe, which is fine here since binds are main-thread only. For background formatting, use java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter (immutable and thread-safe, on API 26+ or via desugaring). Better still, precompute display strings in the mapping layer, off the main thread, as part of the UI model.
  7. Prevention: Review rule: extension properties must be O(1) with no allocation, otherwise make them a function. Add a LeakCanary check in debug builds and instrumented tests. Run a Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric on the list scroll in CI on a low-end device profile. Ban global maps keyed by Context, Activity or View (lint or review).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No WeakHashMap<Context, Int> band-aid. It's still pointless, since one color is resolved once. No ThreadLocal formatter pool for main-thread-only code, because that's complexity with no benefit. And I wouldn't start with the image loader with zero images on screen.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the locale changes while the screen is open? → The configuration change recreates the Activity and adapter, so the formatter is rebuilt. If you handle config changes yourself, rebuild on onConfigurationChanged.
  • Is val Int.dp (a density conversion extension) a problem too? → Only if it reads Resources.getSystem() and math. That's cheap with no allocation, so it's fine as a property.
  • Expected gain? → Removing about 200 allocations of formatter graphs per second typically removes most bind-time GC. I'd confirm with Macrobenchmark before and after rather than promise a number.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A chat app's val Long.relativeTime created a DateUtils formatter per access across 3 text fields per row. Caching per adapter cut slow frames on low-end devices roughly in half in the benchmark run.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Generic RecyclerView tips, or chases the image loader.
  • Hire: Spots the per-access formatter allocation and the leaking map, and caches per adapter.
  • Strong hire: Explains it via "no backing field", does the allocation math, handles thread-safety and locale, verifies with profiler, LeakCanary and Macrobenchmark, and sets a review rule for extension properties.

questions.contextHtml:
Your app (3.5M DAU) forwards analytics events to your own ingestion backend as well as to a vendor SDK. Years ago someone wrote:

// EventExt.kt
fun VendorEvent.toJson(): String = buildJsonObject {
    put("name", name); put("ts", timestampMs); put("props", JsonObject(props.mapValues { JsonPrimitive(it.value) }))
}.toString()

class EventForwarder(private val backend: IngestApi) {
    fun forward(e: VendorEvent) = backend.send(e.toJson())
}

You upgrade the vendor SDK from 4.x to 5.0 (a Java library) and ship to a 20% staged rollout. Within 2 hours your ingestion service's schema-rejection rate goes from 0.02% to 38% for the new app version. The rejected payloads look like {"event_name":"checkout","time":"2026-10-30T10:12:01Z","attributes":{...}}. The build was green. CI shows about 1,200 compiler warnings, as usual. Red herring: the SDK release notes mention "new batching", and the backend team suspects batching changed payload sizes.
questions.promptHtml: What happened? How do you handle the live rollout, and how do you make this upgrade (and future ones) safe?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The vendor changed their format, ask them to revert," or "batching is breaking payloads". It doesn't realize that our own code now calls their method.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did any code in EventForwarder change? (No.) Does VendorEvent in 5.0 now have a toJson() member? (I'd check the API diff or decompile.) Can the backend accept both shapes temporarily? Is the 38% only the forwarded stream, not vendor traffic?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the staged rollout at 20% in Play Console. If the backend can, add a temporary adapter that accepts the vendor shape for the affected app version, so data isn't lost. Otherwise, rejected events are buffered or replayed only if the client retries, and I'd confirm that.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) SDK 5.0 added a member toJson() with the same signature. The member wins, so our extension is silently bypassed. Strongest, because the rejected payload is clearly a different schema produced on the client. (b) Batching changed the envelope, but the per-event field names differ, not just the wrapper. (c) A serialization library change. Nothing changed on our side.
  4. How I'd verify each: Search the build log for "Extension is shadowed by a member: public open fun toJson()" in EventExt.kt. Run javap -public on the new SDK class, or check the IDE: the extension declaration shows the warning and the call site navigates to the SDK member. Write a unit test asserting forward() output against a golden JSON.
  5. Root cause: Kotlin resolves member functions before extensions. When 5.0 introduced VendorEvent.toJson(): String, every e.toJson() call site rebound to the member at compile time. The extension still exists, so nothing failed. The compiler emitted only a warning, lost among 1,200 others. The output changed to the vendor's schema.
  6. Fix: Short-term (hotfix): 
    fun VendorEvent.toIngestJson(): String = buildJsonObject {        // distinctive, unshadowable name
    put("name", name); put("ts", timestampMs)
    put("props", JsonObject(props.mapValues { JsonPrimitive(it.value) }))
}.toString()

class EventForwarder(private val backend: IngestApi) {
    fun forward(e: VendorEvent) = backend.send(e.toIngestJson())
}
    Long-term: map vendor types to our own IngestEvent data class at the boundary, serialized with kotlinx.serialization, so our wire format never depends on a third-party type's API surface.
  7. Prevention: Promote "extension shadowed by member" to an error. Get the warning count to near zero first, or at least fail on new warnings via a baseline. Use golden-file contract tests for every outgoing payload, run on dependency bumps. Have a dependency-upgrade checklist: diff the public API (for example with javap or the binary-compatibility-validator dump for Kotlin libs) on classes we extend. Monitor the ingestion rejection rate by app version, with alerting.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't pin the old SDK forever, since that misses security fixes. I wouldn't ask the vendor to remove a member, which isn't reasonable. And I wouldn't fix it by calling the extension explicitly as EventExtKt.toJson(e). That works in Java, but in Kotlin the fix is the rename. Hacks like importing with an alias don't beat a member either.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would an import alias import com.app.toJson as ourToJson fix it? → Yes, because e.ourToJson() no longer matches the member's name. It's equivalent to a rename, but less discoverable, so I'd rename.
  • What if the vendor added toJson(pretty: Boolean = false)? → A member with a default param is still applicable to toJson(), so the member wins again. That's another reason for distinctive names.
  • How do you recover the lost 2 hours of events? → Only if the client persisted and retries on 4xx. Otherwise, reconcile from the vendor's copy if contracts allow. Document the gap.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fun Date.format() extension was shadowed after a team moved to a wrapper type that had its own format(), and receipts printed in US format for a week. The lesson stuck: no generic verbs as extension names on types you don't control.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames the vendor or batching, and doesn't know member-over-extension resolution.
  • Hire: Identifies the shadowing, renames, and halts the rollout.
  • Strong hire: Handles rollout and data recovery, verifies via the warning and the API diff, adds contract tests and warnings-as-errors with a baseline, and designs an anti-corruption mapping layer so the wire format is ours.

questions.contextHtml: Your Android org is growing from 15 to about 150 engineers across 60 Gradle modules. Every feature module depends on :core:common, which holds 420 public extensions: 95 on Context, 70 on View, 60 on String, plus Fragment, Flow and others. Symptoms: changing any file in :core:common triggers rebuilds of 58 modules (incremental build p50 goes from 40 s to 4.5 min after such a change). Three different fun Context.toast(...) exist in different packages with different default durations. String.isValid() means "valid email" in one package and "non-blank" in another. New hires complain that autocomplete on String shows 60 project suggestions. A tech lead proposes "one extensions module per type: :ext:context, :ext:view, :ext:string".
questions.promptHtml: How would you restructure this for a 10x larger team? Evaluate the tech lead's proposal.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Split by type like the tech lead said," or "delete duplicates". Splitting by receiver type keeps everyone depending on everything, and doesn't fix ambiguity or ownership.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which extensions are used by how many modules? (Get a usage census with a script or IDE "find usages", or a Gradle dependency analysis plugin.) Which carry domain meaning vs pure platform convenience? Is there a design system module already? Do any modules publish to other apps as libraries (API stability)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Freeze additions to :core:common (CODEOWNERS plus a review rule). Mark known-duplicate extensions @Deprecated(level = WARNING) with ReplaceWith pointing to the chosen implementation, which gives IDE-assisted migration.
  3. Hypotheses (problems), ranked: (a) Organizing by receiver type instead of by domain or capability makes a god-module, causing build fan-out and ambiguous semantics. (b) Public-by-default visibility pollutes autocomplete. (c) No ownership, so duplication and drift.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run a usage census to find the share used by fewer than 3 modules (likely most, and those move to their feature). Use Gradle build scans to measure rebuild fan-out before and after. Grep for duplicate signatures (fun Context.toast).
  5. Root cause: Extensions are cheap to write and look "global", so they accumulated in the one module everybody already depended on. Organizing by receiver type is technical, not semantic. String.isValid() belongs to the email-validation domain, not to "String". Any change invalidates the ABI of a module 58 others consume.
  6. Fix:
    • By capability, not by receiver: :core:ui (View/Compose helpers owned by the design system team), :core:format (money/date formatting with explicit Formatter classes), :domain:auth (email validation as EmailAddress.parse(), a value type instead of String.isValid()), feature-local internal helpers inside each feature.
    • Visibility: internal by default, and explicit API mode on core modules, so public surface is deliberate.
    • Naming rules: no generic verbs on platform types (isValid, format, toast with hidden defaults). Replace stringly-typed domain extensions with value classes.
    • Migration: Deprecate with ReplaceWith, then automated IDE refactors module by module, then delete after N releases.
    @Deprecated("Ambiguous; use EmailAddress.parse", ReplaceWith("EmailAddress.parse(this) != null", "com.app.auth.EmailAddress"))
fun String.isValid(): Boolean = EmailAddress.parse(this) != null
  7. Prevention: CODEOWNERS on core modules. Detekt or a custom lint rule flagging new public top-level extensions on Context/View/String in core modules. Track ABI with binary-compatibility-validator dumps so public API changes are visible in PRs. Watch a build-fan-out dashboard from build scans.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The tech lead's per-type split reduces file size but not coupling. Almost every feature uses Context helpers, so everyone still depends on :ext:context, and the ambiguity remains. I also wouldn't do a big-bang rename across 60 modules in one PR, because the merge conflicts would stall 150 engineers. Some duplication across features is acceptable. Shared ownership is more costly than two 3-line helpers.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Do extensions in a module affect build speed differently from regular functions? → No, it's the same. The issue is ABI churn in a widely depended-on module. Kotlin's compile avoidance helps only when the ABI is unchanged.
  • How do you choose which toast wins? → The design-system owner picks one with explicit params (no hidden defaults), and the others get deprecated with ReplaceWith.
  • Should Compose Modifier extensions follow the same rule? → Yes. Shared modifiers live in the design-system module, and one-off modifiers stay private/internal in the feature.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's fun View.visible() existed in 4 variants. One also set alpha = 1f, and screens behaved differently depending on the import. A deprecation-plus-ReplaceWith campaign unified them in two sprints.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Accepts the per-type split, and has no migration or ownership plan.
  • Hire: Moves to capability-based modules, deduplicates, and uses internal.
  • Strong hire: Uses data (census, build scans), adds deprecation with ReplaceWith migration, value classes for stringly domain logic, explicit API/BCV, CODEOWNERS, and a staged rollout that doesn't block 150 engineers. Explains why the per-type split fails.

questions.contextHtml:
A file-upload screen shows progress. Crashlytics reports a new crash cluster of about 0.09% of upload sessions (about 1,100 crashes per day), on all API levels, more on 8-core devices:

Fatal Exception: java.lang.NullPointerException
    at com.app.upload.UploadManager.onProgress(UploadManager.kt:41)
    at com.app.upload.ProgressRequestBody$writeTo$1.invoke(ProgressRequestBody.kt:28)
    at okio.ForwardingSink.write(...)
    ... OkHttp Dispatcher thread "OkHttp https://upload.app.com/..."
class UploadManager {
    private var listener: ProgressListener? = null

    fun attach(l: ProgressListener) { listener = l }         // main thread, Fragment onStart
    fun detach() { listener = null }                          // main thread, Fragment onStop

    fun onProgress(percent: Int) {                            // called on OkHttp thread
        listener?.let {
            if (percent % 5 == 0) listener!!.onProgress(percent)   // line 41
        }
    }
}

A teammate notes the crash "started after the Kotlin upgrade", because the exception type changed from KotlinNullPointerException in older builds.
questions.promptHtml: What's the bug, why does it only crash sometimes, and what's the correct fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a try/catch around it," or "the Kotlin upgrade broke !!". Both miss the check-then-act race caused by re-reading the property.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which thread calls onProgress? (OkHttp's writer thread.) Do crashes correlate with users leaving the screen mid-upload (onStop → detach)? Did the code change, or just the exception class?
  2. Immediate mitigation: A one-line fix in the next hotfix, using it. The crash rate is low but user-visible during uploads, so it's worth a point release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A race: listener?.let reads the field, then listener!! re-reads it. detach() on main can null it in between. (b) The Kotlin upgrade "broke" !!, which is a red herring. Since Kotlin 1.4, !! throws java.lang.NullPointerException instead of KotlinNullPointerException. Only the exception class name changed, so the cluster got a new Crashlytics signature and looked "new". (c) Leaked UploadManager instances. Possible, but not needed to explain the NPE.
  4. How I'd verify each: Correlate crash timestamps with Fragment onStop breadcrumbs. A stress test: call detach() in a loop while another thread calls onProgress(), which reproduces quickly. Check the Crashlytics issue history to see the older KotlinNullPointerException cluster with a similar rate.
  5. Root cause: ?.let captures the value into it exactly once. But the body ignores it and reads the mutable property again with !!. The two reads happen on the OkHttp thread while detach() writes on main. If the write lands between them, the second read is null, so !! throws. More cores mean more true parallelism, which explains the device skew. Without @Volatile there's also no visibility guarantee, though that's secondary here.
  6. Fix: 
    @Volatile private var listener: ProgressListener? = null   // visibility across threads

fun onProgress(percent: Int) {
    if (percent % 5 != 0) return
    val l = listener ?: return            // single read
    mainHandler.post { l.onProgress(percent) }   // deliver on main; UI listener expects main
}
    Even the fixed version can deliver one update to a just-detached listener (snapshot semantics). That's harmless if the listener checks lifecycle, and a reason to move progress to a StateFlow collected with lifecycle awareness (see the Flow and synchronization chunks).
  7. Prevention: Code-review rule: inside x?.let { }, never reference x again, only it. Detekt has UnnecessaryLet and related rules, and the IDE flags !! after a null check on the same property in some cases, but a review rule is more reliable. Ban !! in shared-state code via detekt UnsafeCallOnNullableType. Write a multi-threaded stress test for listener attach and detach.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No try/catch for NPE, which hides the race and keeps calling into dead UI. No synchronized around the UI callback, since holding a lock while calling foreign code invites deadlocks. A single read plus main-thread delivery is enough.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is listener?.onProgress(percent) alone safe? → Yes for the NPE, because it's a single read. But it still calls the listener on the OkHttp thread, which is wrong for UI.
  • Why did the old code "work" in debug? → Debug builds and emulators had fewer cores and slower writes, so the race window rarely hit.
  • Would lateinit help? → No. It can't be reset to null, and accessing it uninitialized throws.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A media controller had player?.let { player!!.seekTo(...) } in a sensor callback. The "fix" was another null check, and it crashed a month later at the same line. The real fix was a single read and thread confinement.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Wraps it in try/catch, or blames the Kotlin upgrade.
  • Hire: Spots the re-read race and uses it or a local val.
  • Strong hire: Explains the !! exception-type change (the red herring) and the device skew, adds visibility and main-thread delivery, notes snapshot semantics, and adds review and detekt prevention.

questions.contextHtml:
The analytics team reports that for the last 3 weeks, 41% of button_click events have screen = null and another 12% have values like com.app.databinding.ItemCartBinding@7f2a1c. Dashboards that rank screens by engagement are now useless. Nothing crashes. Three weeks ago a "tracking helper" was added to the shared base Fragment used by 80 screens:

abstract class BaseFragment : Fragment() {
    @Inject lateinit var analytics: Analytics

    protected fun View.onClickTracked(event: String, action: () -> Unit) {
        setOnClickListener {
            analytics.log(event, mapOf("screen" to tag, "id" to id))
            action()
        }
    }
}
// usage in CartFragment
binding.checkout.onClickTracked("button_click") { viewModel.checkout() }

Fragments are added with replace(R.id.container, CartFragment(), "Cart"). Red herrings: the analytics SDK was also upgraded that month, and someone suspects ProGuard/R8 stripping fragment tags.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose this. Why null for some events and binding objects for others? Fix it so the class of bug is designed out.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "R8 is stripping the tags, add keep rules," or "the SDK upgrade changed map serialization". It doesn't recognize that tag and id resolve to the View, not the Fragment.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do the bad events correlate with the release that added onClickTracked? (Yes, 3 weeks.) What are the id values? (I'd bet they're View resource ids like 2131362001, not fragment container ids.) Are the binding-object values from list rows, where adapters setTag(binding)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the helper to read the fragment's screen name explicitly. Ask the analytics team to mark the 3-week window as unreliable for screen and backfill where possible. Events have the View id, which can be mapped to screens through a resource-id lookup table for the affected build.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Implicit receiver precedence inside a member extension: tag and id resolve to the extension receiver (View) before the dispatch receiver (Fragment). This fits both symptoms. Buttons without a tag give null, and list rows whose root View is tagged with a binding give the binding's toString(). (b) R8 stripping, but fragment tags are runtime strings, and R8 doesn't remove them. (c) The SDK upgrade: the values are wrong before reaching the SDK.
  4. How I'd verify each: Read the code. In the IDE, Ctrl/Cmd-click tag inside onClickTracked and it navigates to View.getTag(). A unit or Robolectric test: a fragment with tag "Cart" and a tracked button, asserting the logged screen == "Cart", which fails now. Check whether the event's id matches View ids in R.txt for that build.
  5. Root cause: onClickTracked is a member extension with two implicit receivers: the extension receiver View and the dispatch receiver BaseFragment. Unqualified names resolve on the extension receiver first. View.tag (Any?) and View.id (Int) exist, so they shadow Fragment.tag (String?) and Fragment.id. There's no type error because the map is Map<String, Any?>. So most buttons log null, and rows tagged with view-binding objects log ItemCartBinding@....
  6. Fix: 
    abstract class BaseFragment : Fragment() {
    @Inject lateinit var analytics: Analytics
    protected abstract val screenName: String          // explicit, distinctive, not a platform name

    protected fun View.onClickTracked(event: String, action: () -> Unit) {
        setOnClickListener {
            analytics.log(event, mapOf("screen" to screenName, "viewId" to resources.getResourceEntryName(id)))
            action()
        }
    }
}
    screenName doesn't exist on View, so it can't be shadowed. this@BaseFragment.tag would also fix it, but fragment tags are optional and inconsistent across 80 screens. An explicit abstract property makes every screen declare its name (a compile error if it's missing). Also type the analytics payload, like ClickEvent(screen: String, viewId: String) instead of Map<String, Any?>. Then View.tag: Any? wouldn't have compiled into a String field at all. (getResourceEntryName throws for View.NO_ID, so guard it or log the raw id in real code.)
  7. Prevention: Review rule: inside member extensions and this-receiver scope functions, references to outer-class members must be qualified, or use names that don't exist on the receiver. Prefer typed event schemas over Map<String, Any?>. Add an analytics contract test per base helper. Add a data-quality alert on the null rate for screen (it should be about 0%), which would have fired on day 1, not week 3.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No R8 keep rules (wrong cause). I wouldn't drop the member extension entirely: button.onClickTracked { } reads well, and the scoping (only callable inside BaseFragment) is useful. The fix is explicit naming and typing. I also wouldn't make every fragment pass the screen name at each call site, which is error-prone across 80 screens.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would @DslMarker have prevented it? → No. DslMarker restricts implicit access to outer receivers of the same marked DSL. Here the problem is that the inner receiver wins, which is normal resolution.
  • What if View gained a screenName property in a future API? → A member of the extension receiver would shadow it again. Use names unlikely to collide, or qualify with this@BaseFragment, which is the bulletproof form.
  • Why didn't code review catch it? → tag reads naturally in a Fragment. Reviewers resolve names by the file's class, not the lambda's receiver. That's why the rule is mechanical (qualify or rename).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A with(binding) { } block in a Fragment referenced context, and it resolved to binding.root.context. That was harmless, until it was requireView() vs root during a transition, which logged a misleading lifecycle state. Same class of bug: implicit receiver precedence.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Pursues R8 or the SDK, and can't explain name resolution.
  • Hire: Identifies View vs Fragment tag/id resolution and qualifies with this@BaseFragment.
  • Strong hire: Explains the two-receiver precedence, accounts for both symptom shapes (null vs binding objects), designs out the bug (abstract screenName, typed schema), proposes backfill via resource-id mapping, and adds a data-quality alert.
